notes.claim: An ideal transformer assumes all the magnetic field lines stay in the core, so the same flux links every turn of both windings.
A good real transformer can have losses as low as 1% of the transmitted power.
Transformers cannot change DC voltages, because they work by Faraday's law of induction.
Around a long straight wire carrying current, the field lines form circular loops centred on the wire.
A solenoid, a long coil of wire carrying current, makes a field that resembles a bar magnet's.
Magnetic flux measures how much of a magnetic field passes perpendicular through an area, and a change in it induces a voltage.

Round a long straight wire the flux density is B = μ0 I ÷ (2π r), where μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A is the magnetic constant (the permeability of free space); with B in mT and r in mm this is 0.2 × current in A ÷ distance in mm.
Current times turns, in ampere-turns, is the magnetomotive force that drives flux round a magnetic circuit, much as voltage drives current round an electric one.
Iron's permeability is far higher than air's; one source puts iron's relative permeability at about 5000, so the same ampere-turns give far more flux through an iron core.
At saturation a rise in magnetic field intensity gives only a minimal rise in flux density, so more current buys little extra flux.
Reluctance S = F ÷ Φ, so the flux is the ampere-turns divided by the reluctance: Ohm's law for a magnetic circuit. (added for i2, review fix)
Ferromagnetic materials contain domains, groups of aligned dipoles, that align with an applied field; when the field is removed the material stays magnetised. (added for i2, review fix)
Saturation is the point where most of the domains are aligned, so more current gets little more. (added for i2, review fix)
The hysteresis loop's area is the energy lost as heat per unit volume each cycle, so a thinner loop loses less. (added for i2, review fix)
Eddy loss per unit volume in a thin lamination goes as the square of its thickness, so halving the thickness quarters it. (added for i2, review fix)
Core steel is alloyed with silicon, which lowers its conductivity and so its eddy loss. (added for i2, review fix)
Hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the core are no-load losses, the iron loss (SECONDARY source). (added for i2, review fix)
The magnetic constant μ0 is 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m (= T m/A) to within 2.3 parts in 10¹⁰. (added for i2, review fix)
With an unchanging flux there is no induced emf in the loop and no current from it.
A sinusoidal supply voltage on a coil is tied by a definite relation to the flux density in the core and the core's size.
Transformers cannot change DC voltages, because they work by Faraday's law of induction.
In an ideal transformer the ratio of secondary to primary voltage equals the ratio of turns in the windings.
The current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio; a transformer does not create power or consume it, so power in equals power out in the ideal case.
The ideal case assumes the same flux links every turn of both windings, which is why the voltage ratio follows the turns ratio.
A transformer has a no-load loss, present whenever it is energised whatever the load, and a load loss that goes with the square of the loading.
The open-circuit (no-load) test measures the iron loss; the short-circuit test, run at rated current, measures the copper loss.
A good real transformer can have losses as low as 1% of the transmitted power.
A lagging power factor load lowers a transformer's secondary terminal voltage, while a leading one raises it.
A transformer with lower impedance may give better voltage regulation but can deliver substantially more current into a downstream fault.
At 5% impedance, full primary voltage would drive 20 times (100 divided by 5) the full-load secondary current through a solid short on the secondary terminals.
A transformer's percentage impedance is also called its impedance voltage, expressed as a percentage (Z%).
In clock notation the high-voltage phasor sits at 12 and the number gives the hour of the low-voltage phasor, each hour being 30 degrees.
Dyn11 means a delta high-voltage winding, a star low-voltage winding with its neutral brought out, and a displacement of 11 times 30, or 330 degrees.
Eleven o'clock is 330 degrees, the same as the low-voltage side leading the high-voltage side by 30 degrees.
Transformers to be paralleled need matching vector groups, so their output voltages are in phase and no short circuit occurs.
Dyn11 is read by most sources as the low-voltage side leading by 30 degrees (330 degrees lagging), but one maker's page calls it a 30 degree lag.
notes.contested: Ryan Transformers (and the clock convention it cites) read 11 as LV leading HV by 30 degrees; HD Transformer's page calls it a 30 degree lag of LV behind HV.

notes.claim: Transformers to be paralleled should preferably have the same voltage ratio, rated power, short-circuit impedance and vector group.
Paralleling transformers whose power ratio is two or more is not recommended.
Transformer inrush currents are predominantly due to saturation of the core.
Inrush can reach instantaneous peaks of 8 to 30 times the full-load current.

With primary current flowing, an open-circuited current transformer secondary can cause high voltages, as much as 4000 V measured on large-core CTs, and the open secondary drives the core into saturation.
An isolation transformer has no electrical connection between primary and secondary; an autotransformer has a physical electrical connection between them.
A US rule for ships requires at least two independent ship's service transformers, the rest able to carry the service loads with the largest out.
Winding insulation must suit the system feeding it; ungrounded systems require a fully insulated winding.
